summary: Networks sometimes run several redundant sources of the same multicast stream for high availability. This document describes how Ethernet VPNs (EVPN) can handle such redundant sources, so receivers get the traffic reliably and efficiently.

eli5.summary: Imagine two radio stations broadcasting the same show so one can keep playing if the other fails. This explains how the network handles that without confusing listeners.

questions: what is evpn multicast source redundancy
what is warm standby in evpn
what is hot standby in evpn
what is a single flow group
subtitle: How EVPN networks keep two or more copies of the same multicast stream from reaching a receiver twice.

tldr.problem: When several redundant sources send the same multicast flow into an EVPN tenant network for high availability, receivers can get duplicate packets, and existing EVPN multicast procedures give no way to prevent that.
tldr.mechanism: Two solutions are defined. In Warm Standby the upstream PEs elect a Single Forwarder using S-PMSI A-D routes. In Hot Standby every source's traffic is sent with an ESI label, and each downstream PE discards packets that carry the wrong label.
tldr.outcome: Warm Standby saves bandwidth but fails over more slowly. Hot Standby fails over fast but uses more bandwidth and requires support on the downstream PEs.

today: RFC 9856 is a Proposed Standard published in September 2025. It does not obsolete or update any other RFC, and no RFC has obsoleted or updated it.

sections.title: Redundant Multicast Sources in EVPN
sections.content:
Ethernet VPNs (EVPNs) support IP multicast inside one subnet (RFC 9251) and between subnets of one tenant (RFC 9625, called OISM). Neither, nor conventional IP multicast, handles the case where a multicast group carries several flows, one from each redundant source, and each receiver should get only one. Normally the receiving application is expected to cope with duplicates.

In classic PIM or MVPN networks, a workaround is to give all redundant sources the same IP address, often an anycast address, so each receiver ends up on at most one source-specific tree. The RFC says this suits Warm Standby, but it does not work for Hot Standby, causes trouble when sources must be reachable by unicast, and fails with OISM where there may be only (*,G) state and no Rendezvous Point.

This document extends RFC 9251 and RFC 9625 with procedures for EVPN Provider Edge (PE) routers so receivers do not see duplicates when two or more sources send identical flows into the tenant domain. Other multicast solutions are out of scope.
sections.eli5: When two sources send the same show, the network needs a rule so you do not get it twice. Older tricks do not work in this kind of network, so this RFC adds new ones.

sections.title: Multicast Delivery and Multi-Homed Sources
sections.content:
In an EVPN tenant, the source and receivers of a flow may sit in the same Broadcast Domain (BD), which is intra-subnet forwarding, or in different BDs, which is inter-subnet forwarding. Delivery can use an Inclusive tree to every PE of the BD, or a Selective tree (S-PMSI) to just the PEs that sent Selective Multicast Ethernet Tag (SMET) routes for the flow. In OISM, flows are sent in the context of the source BD, or in the Supplementary Broadcast Domain (SBD) for PEs not attached to the source BD.

A single source attached to two PEs through a multi-homed Ethernet Segment does not cause duplicates, because EVPN multi-homing ensures that only one upstream PE forwards a given flow at a time. The SMET route keeps all upstream PEs in the segment holding state, so the backup can take over immediately.

The RFC argues that this resiliency is not enough for critical applications. It therefore assumes redundant G-sources: separate hosts or routers sending the same Single Flow Group, possibly in the same or different BDs, single-homed or multi-homed, with receivers anywhere in the tenant. The PEs must make sure receivers see no duplicates.
sections.eli5: Having one source plugged into two network doors is already safe. But for important shows, there are two whole sources, and the network must make sure you only see one of them at a time.

sections.title: Two Solutions Based on Single Flow Groups
sections.content:
The key idea is the Single Flow Group (SFG): a multicast group that carries a single flow, even though several sources may send it. An SFG is written as (*,G), meaning any source sending to G is a redundant G-source, or as (S,G) where S is a prefix of any length, so only sources matching the prefix count. For instance, with the IPv4 prefix 192.0.2.0/30, sources 192.0.2.1 and 192.0.2.2 are redundant, but 192.0.2.10 is not.

Warm Standby (WS) is an upstream-PE solution. The PEs attached to redundant sources elect a Single Forwarder (SF); non-SF PEs discard the flow arriving on their local attachment circuits. Downstream PEs do not take part.

Hot Standby (HS) relies on downstream PEs. Upstream PEs tag each SFG packet with an ESI label for its source, every PE receives all copies, and each downstream PE keeps only the copy from its chosen source.

On choosing: WS is more bandwidth-efficient but has longer failover times, and only the upstream PEs need to support it. HS is recommended when fast failover is needed and the extra bandwidth is acceptable. A system is not required to support both, and if it implements one, support for the other is OPTIONAL.
sections.eli5: Warm Standby is like the school letting only one of two identical announcers talk at a time. Hot Standby is like both announcers talking, and your TV only listening to one of them.

sections.title: BGP EVPN Extensions
sections.content:
Two extensions are introduced. First, a new Single Flow Group flag in the Multicast Flags Extended Community, registered by IANA as bit 4. It is set in S-PMSI A-D routes that carry (*,G) or (S,G) SFG information.

Second, the Hot Standby solution attaches one or more ESI Label Extended Communities to an S-PMSI A-D route. They carry the ESI labels of the sources behind the SFG. Only the ESI label value matters here, and the Flags field MUST be set to 0x00 on transmission and ignored on reception. RFC 7432 uses this community with the A-D per ES route; this document allows it to appear several times, with different label values, on one S-PMSI A-D route.
sections.eli5: The routers pass notes to each other over BGP. This RFC adds two new kinds of marking: one that says "this is a single-flow group" and one that carries a label for each source.

sections.title: Warm Standby Procedure
sections.content:
Upstream PEs are first configured with the groups that carry an SFG and the BDs that may host redundant sources. When a PE gets the first multicast packet for a configured SFG in a BD, it MUST advertise an S-PMSI A-D route: (*,G) for an any-source SFG, or (S,G) for a source-prefix SFG. The route MUST carry the BD route target (plus the SBD route target in OISM), the Multicast Flags Extended Community with the SFG flag, and the Designated Forwarder Election Extended Community. It has a PMSI Tunnel Attribute unless the tunnel is IR, AR or BIER. The PE MUST withdraw the route when the SFG traffic stops, and an inactivity timer is RECOMMENDED.

PEs that see S-PMSI A-D routes for the same SFG (same tenant, source length, source, group length and group) run a Single Forwarder election per the DF election community (RFC 8584). The same algorithm MUST be used on all upstream PEs, and in OISM the Default DF Election Algorithm MUST NOT be used if sources are in BDs with different Ethernet Tags. On a mismatch, the lowest PE IP address (the Originator Address) breaks the tie.

Then a Reverse Path Forwarding check applies. Non-SF PEs MUST discard (*,G) or (S,G) packets received on local attachment circuits, and the SF MUST forward them from one and only one local circuit.

In the RFC's OISM example, PE1 has preference 200 and PE2 has preference 100, so PE1 is elected. If S1, its circuit or PE1 fails, PE1's S-PMSI A-D route is withdrawn and PE2 becomes the Single Forwarder. The single-BD example works the same way, but the routes carry only the BD route target because there is no SBD.
sections.eli5: The two source-side routers hold a quick election. The winner passes the show along and the loser throws its copy away. If the winner breaks, the loser notices and takes over.

sections.title: Hot Standby Procedure
sections.content:
In Hot Standby, each redundant source MUST be tied to an Ethernet Segment on the upstream PEs, single-homed or multi-homed; its ESI is the S-ESI. Upstream PEs MUST advertise an S-PMSI A-D route for each SFG, triggered by configuration and not by traffic, with ESI Label Extended Communities that match the labels in their EVPN A-D per ES routes. All packets for one source MUST carry the same S-ESI label, even across multi-homing PEs, and different sources MUST get different labels. The labels are Domain-wide Common Block (DCB) labels, as in RFC 9573.

Downstream PEs need no configuration for SFGs. After importing A-D per ES routes for different S-ESes, a PE MUST pick a primary S-ES by local policy (the example uses the lowest ESI value) and add a Reverse Path Forwarding check that discards packets for the group not carrying the primary S-ESI label. Different downstream PEs may choose different sources.

When forwarding, the upstream PE puts the S-ESI label at the bottom of the label stack. With P2MP or BIER this adds no new data path requirement. With IR or AR the label is pushed on packets for all PEs in the tenant, not only those sharing the ES, so every downstream PE gets each packet with a label.

If the last A-D per EVI or A-D per ES route for the primary S-ES is withdrawn, the downstream PE immediately selects a new primary. Withdrawing all A-D per ES routes of an S-ES lets a PE update the check for all tenants using it at once. Withdrawal of the last S-PMSI A-D route for the SFG SHOULD remove the check. Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (BFD) MAY also be used to monitor the multipoint tunnels (RFC 9780).
sections.eli5: Here every source stamps its packets with its own colored sticker. Every viewer's router chooses a favorite color and drops packets with other stickers. If the favorite source goes away, the router picks a new favorite right away.

sections.title: DCB Labels in the ESI Label Community
sections.content:
RFC 9573 assumes DCB labels apply only to multipoint-to-multipoint, point-to-multipoint or BIER tunnels. This document additionally allows DCB-allocated ESI labels to be used with IR tunnels and by PEs that do not use DCB-allocated PMSI labels.

This is signaled in the EVPN A-D per ES routes by adding an ESI-DCB flag to the ESI Label Extended Community or by adding the Context-Specific Label Space ID extended community. The ESI-DCB flag is bit 5 of the Flags octet in the community, and when set it means the ESI label is a DCB label. A label also counts as a DCB label if the PE advertised a PMSI label that is a DCB label.
sections.eli5: The labels are chosen from a list that all the routers agree on in advance. A single flag says "this label comes from the shared list."

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The security considerations of RFC 9625 apply here too. The RFC adds that Warm Standby is lighter on the control plane and so has a low impact on PE processing, while Hot Standby adds more burden on the control plane of all PEs of the tenant that have sources and receivers.
sections.eli5: Warm Standby gives the routers less gossip to keep track of. Hot Standby makes every router keep more notes.
